entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13152"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 11</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Zech.11.1-Zech.11.17">Zec 11:1-17</reference>. Destruction of the Second Temple and Jewish Polity for the Rejection of Messiah.</title> <div sID="gen24793" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13152"/><hi type="bold">1. Open thy doors, O Lebanon--</hi>that is, the temple so called, as being constructed of cedars of Lebanon, or as being lofty and conspicuous like that mountain (compare <reference osisRef="Ezek.17.3">Eze 17:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hab.2.17">Ha 2:17</reference>). Forty years before the destruction of the temple, the tract called "Massecheth Joma" states, its doors of their own accord opened, and Rabbi Johanan in alarm said, I know that thy desolation is impending according to Zechariah's prophecy. Calvin supposes Lebanon to refer to Judea, described by its north boundary: "Lebanon," the route by which the Romans, according to Josephus, gradually advanced towards Jerusalem. Moore, from Hengstenberg, refers the passage to the civil war which caused the calling in of the Romans, who, like a storm sweeping through the land from Lebanon, deprived Judea of its independence. Thus the passage forms a fit introduction to the prediction as to Messiah born when Judea became a Roman province. But the weight of authority is for the former view. <div eID="gen24793" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13153"/><div sID="gen24794" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13153"/><hi type="bold">2. fir tree ... cedar--</hi>if even the cedars (the highest in the state) are not spared, how much less the fir trees (the lowest)!<div eID="gen24794" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24795" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">forest of ... vintage--</hi>As the vines are stripped of their grapes in the vintage (compare <reference osisRef="Joel.3.13">Joe 3:13</reference>), so the forest of Lebanon "is come down," stripped of all its beauty. Rather, "the fortified" or "inaccessible forest" [Maurer]; that is, Jerusalem dense with houses as a thick forest is with trees, and "fortified" with a wall around. Compare <reference osisRef="Mic.3.12">Mi 3:12</reference>, where its desolate state is described as a forest. <div eID="gen24795" type="x-p"/>

Image for Judea "spoiled" of the magnificence of its rulers ("the young lions"). The valley of the Jordan forms a deeper gash than any on the earth. The land at Lake Merom is on a level with the Mediterranean Sea; at the Sea of Tiberias it falls six hundred fifty feet below that level, and to double that depression at the Dead Sea, that is, in all, 1950 feet below the Mediterranean; in twenty miles' interval there is a fall of from three thousand to four thousand feet. <div eID="gen24799" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13155"/><div sID="gen24800" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13155"/>4. The prophet here proceeds to show the cause of the destruction just foretold, namely, the rejection of Messiah.<div eID="gen24800" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24801" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">flock of ... slaughter--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.44.22">Psa 44:22</reference>). God's people doomed to slaughter by the Romans. Zechariah here represents typically Messiah, and performs in vision the actions enjoined: hence the language is in part appropriate to him, but mainly to the Antitype, Messiah. A million and a half perished in the Jewish war, and one million one hundred thousand at the fall of Jerusalem. "Feed" implies that the Jews could not plead ignorance of God's will to execute their sin. Zechariah and the other prophets had by God's appointment "fed" them (<reference osisRef="Acts.20.28">Ac 20:28</reference>) with the word of God, teaching and warning them to escape from coming wrath by repentance: the type of Messiah, the chief Shepherd, who receives the commission of the Father, with whom He is one (<reference osisRef="Zech.11.4">Zec 11:4</reference>); and Himself says (<reference osisRef="Zech.11.7">Zec 11:7</reference>), "I will feed the flock of slaughter." Zechariah did not live to "feed" literally the "flock of slaughter"; Messiah alone "fed" those who, because of their rejection of Him, were condemned to slaughter. Jehovah-Messiah is the speaker. It is He who threatens to inflict the punishments (<reference osisRef="Zech.11.6">Zec 11:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Zech.11.8">8</reference>). The typical breaking of the staff, performed in vision by Zechariah (<reference osisRef="Zech.11.10">Zec 11:10</reference>), is fulfilled in His breaking the covenant with Judah. It is He who was sold for thirty pieces of silver (<reference osisRef="Zech.11.12">Zec 11:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Zech.11.13">13</reference>). <div eID="gen24801" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13156"/><div sID="gen24802" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13156"/><hi type="bold">5. possessors--</hi>The buyers [Maurer], their Roman oppressors, contrasted with "they that sell men." The instruments of God's righteous judgment, and therefore "not holding themselves guilty" (<reference osisRef="Jer.50.7">Jr 50:7</reference>). It is meant that they might use this plea, not that they actually used it. Judah's adversaries felt no compunction in destroying them; and God in righteous wrath against Judah allowed it.<div eID="gen24802" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24803" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">they that sell them--</hi>(Compare <reference osisRef="Zech.11.12">Zec 11:12</reference>). The rulers of Judah, who by their avaricious rapacity and selfishness (<reference osisRef="John.11.48">Joh 11:48</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.11.50">50</reference>) virtually sold their country to Rome. Their covetousness brought on Judea God's visitation by Rome. The climax of this was the sale of the innocent Messiah for thirty pieces of silver. They thought that Jesus was thus sold and their selfish interest secured by the delivery of Him to the Romans for crucifixion; but it was themselves and their country that they thus sold to the Roman possessors."<div eID="gen24803" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24804" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I am rich--</hi>by selling the sheep (<reference osisRef="Deut.29.19">De 29:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.12.8">Ho 12:8</reference>). In short-sighted selfishness they thought they had gained their object, covetous self-aggrandizement (<reference osisRef="Luke.16.14">Lu 16:14</reference>), and hypocritically "thanked" God for their wicked gain (compare <reference osisRef="Luke.18.11">Lu 18:11</reference>).<div eID="gen24804" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24805" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">say ... pity--</hi>In Hebrew it is singular: that is, each of those that sell them saith: Not one of their own shepherds pitieth them. An emphatical mode of expression by which each individual is represented as doing, or not doing, the action of the verb [Henderson]. Hengstenberg refers the singular verbs to Jehovah, the true actor; the wicked shepherds being His unconscious instruments. Compare <reference osisRef="Zech.11.6">Zec 11:6</reference>, For I will no more pity, with the Hebrew "pitieth not" here. <div eID="gen24805" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13157"/><div sID="gen24806" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13157"/>6. Jehovah, in vengeance for their rejection of Messiah, gave them over to intestine feuds and Roman rule. The Zealots and other factious Jews expelled and slew one another by turns at the last invasion by Rome.<div eID="gen24806" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24807" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">his king--</hi>Vespasian or Titus: they themselves (<reference osisRef="John.19.15">Joh 19:15</reference>) had said, unconsciously realizing Zechariah's words, identifying Rome's king with Judah's ("his") king, "We have no king but Cæsar." God took them at their word, and gave them the Roman king, who "smote (literally, 'dashed in pieces') their land," breaking up their polity, when they rejected their true King who would have saved them. <div eID="gen24807" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13158"/><div sID="gen24808" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13158"/><hi type="bold">7. And--</hi>rather, "Accordingly": implying the motive cause which led Messiah to assume the office, namely, the will of the Father (<reference osisRef="Zech.11.4">Zec 11:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Zech.11.5">5</reference>), who pitied the sheep without any true shepherd.<div eID="gen24808" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24809" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I will feed--</hi>"I fed" [Calvin], which comes to the same thing, as the past tense must in Zechariah's time have referred to the event of Messiah's advent then future: the prophets often speaking of the future in vision as already present. It was not My fault, Jehovah implies, that these sheep were not fed; the fault rests solely with you, because ye rejected the grace of God [Calvin].<div eID="gen24809" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24810" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">even you, O poor of the flock--</hi>rather, "in order that (I might feed, that is, save) the poor (humble; compare <reference osisRef="Zech.11.11">Zec 11:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zeph.3.12">Zep 3:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.5.3">Mt 5:3</reference>) of the flock"; literally, not you, but, "therefore (I will feed)" [Moore]. See Margin, "Verily the poor." It is for the sake of the believing remnant that Messiah took charge of the flock, though He would have saved all, if they would have come to Him. They would not come; therefore, as a nation, they are "the flock of (that is, doomed to) slaughter."<div eID="gen24810" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24811" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I took ... two staves--</hi>that is, shepherds' staves or rods (<reference osisRef="Ps.23.4">Psa 23:4</reference>). Symbolizing His assumption of the pastor's office.<div eID="gen24811" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24812" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Beauty--</hi>The Jews' peculiar excellency above other nations (<reference osisRef="Deut.4.7">De 4:7</reference>), God's special manifestation to them (<reference osisRef="Ps.147.19">Psa 147:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.147.20">20</reference>), the glory of the temple ("the beauty of holiness," <reference osisRef="Ps.29.2">Psa 29:2</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Ps.27.4">Psa 27:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.90.17">90:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.20.21">2Ch 20:21</reference>), the "pleasantness" of their land (<reference osisRef="Gen.49.15">Ge 49:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.8.9">Da 8:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.11.16">11:16</reference>), "the glorious land."<div eID="gen24812" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24813" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Bands--</hi>implying the bond of "brotherhood" between Judah and Israel. "Bands," in <reference osisRef="Ps.119.61">Psa 119:61</reference>, Margin, is used for confederate companies: The Easterns in making a confederacy often tie a cord or band as a symbol of it, and untie it when they dissolve the confederacy [Ludovicus De Dieu]. Messiah would have joined Judah and Israel in the bonds of a common faith and common laws (<reference osisRef="Zech.11.14">Zec 11:14</reference>), but they would not; therefore in just retribution He broke "His covenant which He had made with all the people." Alexander, Antiochus Epiphanes, and Pompey were all kept from marring utterly the distinctive "beauty" and "brotherhood" of Judah and Israel, which subsisted more or less so long as the temple stood. But when Jehovah brake the staves, not even Titus could save the temple from his own Roman soldiery, nor was Jurian able to restore it. <div eID="gen24813" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: 7. And-- rather, "Accordingly": implying the motive cause which led Messiah to assume the office, namely, the will of the Father ( Zec 11:4 , 5 ), who pitied the sheep without any true shepherd. I will feed-- "I fed" [Calvin], which comes to the same thing, as the past tense must in Zechariah's time have referred to the event of Messiah's advent then future: the prophets often speaking of the future in vision as already present. It was not My fault, Jehovah implies, that these sheep were not fed; the fault rests solely with you, because ye rejected the grace of God [Calvin]. even you, O poor of the flock-- rather, "in order that (I might feed, that is, save) the poor (humble; compare Zec 11:11 ; Zep 3:12 ; Mt 5:3 ) of the flock"; literally, not you, but, "therefore (I will feed)" [Moore]. See Margin, "Verily the poor." It is for the sake of the believing remnant that Messiah took charge of the flock, though He would have saved all, if they would have come to Him. They would not come; therefore, as a nation, they are "the flock of (that is, doomed to) slaughter." I took ... two staves-- that is, shepherds' staves or rods ( Psa 23:4 ). Symbolizing His assumption of the pastor's office. Beauty-- The Jews' peculiar excellency above other nations ( De 4:7 ), God's special manifestation to them ( Psa 147:19 , 20 ), the glory of the temple ("the beauty of holiness," Psa 29:2 ; compare Psa 27:4 ; 90:17 ; 2Ch 20:21 ), the "pleasantness" of their land ( Ge 49:15 ; Da 8:9 ; 11:16 ), "the glorious land." Bands-- implying the bond of "brotherhood" between Judah and Israel. "Bands," in Psa 119:61 , Margin, is used for confederate companies: The Easterns in making a confederacy often tie a cord or band as a symbol of it, and untie it when they dissolve the confederacy [Ludovicus De Dieu]. Three shepherds ... I cut off--</hi>literally, "to cause to disappear," to destroy so as not to leave a vestige of them. The three shepherds whom Messiah removes are John, Simon, and Eleazar, three leaders of factions in the Jewish war [Drusius]. Refusing Him, they lost all three, in every sense.<div eID="gen24814" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24815" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">one month--</hi>a brief and fixed space of time (<reference osisRef="Hos.5.7">Ho 5:7</reference>). entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13161"/><div sID="gen24820" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13161"/><hi type="bold">10. covenant which I made with all the people--</hi>The covenant made with the whole nation is to hold good no more except to the elect remnant. This is the force of the clause, not as Maurer, and others translate. The covenant which I made with all the nations (not to hurt My elect people, <reference osisRef="Hos.2.18">Ho 2:18</reference>). But the Hebrew is the term for the elect people (Ammim), not that for the Gentile nations (Goiim). The Hebrew plural expresses the great numbers of the Israelite people formerly (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.4.20">1Ki 4:20</reference>). The article is, in the Hebrew, all the or those peoples. His cutting asunder the staff "Beauty," implies the setting aside of the outward symbols of the Jews distinguishing excellency above the Gentiles (see on <reference osisRef="Zech.11.7">Zec 11:7</reference>) as God's own people. <div eID="gen24820" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13162"/><div sID="gen24821" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13162"/><hi type="bold">11. poor ... knew--</hi>The humble, godly remnant knew by the event the truth of the prediction and of Messiah's mission. I said--</hi>The prophet here represents the person of Jehovah-Messiah.<div eID="gen24823" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24824" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">If ye think good--</hi>literally, "If it be good in your eyes." Glancing at their self-sufficient pride in not deigning to give Him that return which His great love in coming down to them from heaven merited, namely, their love and obedience. "My price"; my reward for pastoral care, both during the whole of Israel's history from the Exodus, and especially the three and a half years of Messiah's ministry. He speaks as their "servant," which He was to them in order to fulfil the Father's will (<reference osisRef="Phil.2.7">Php 2:7</reference>).<div eID="gen24824" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24825" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">if not, forbear--</hi>They withheld that which He sought as His only reward, their love; yet He will not force them, but leave His cause with God (<reference osisRef="Isa.49.4">Is 49:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.49.5">5</reference>). Compare the type Jacob cheated of his wages by Laban, but leaving his cause in the hands of God (<reference osisRef="Gen.31.41">Ge 31:41</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.31.42">42</reference>).<div eID="gen24825" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24826" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">So ... thirty pieces of silver--</hi>thirty shekels. A freeman was rated at twice that sum. <div eID="gen24826" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13164"/><div sID="gen24827" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13164"/><hi type="bold">13. Cast it unto the potter--</hi>proverbial: Throw it to the temple potter, the most suitable person to whom to cast the despicable sum, plying his trade as he did in the polluted valley (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.10">2Ki 23:10</reference>) of Hinnom, because it furnished him with the most suitable clay. This same valley, and the potter's shop, were made the scene of symbolic actions by Jeremiah (<reference osisRef="Jer.18.1-Jer.19.15">Jr 18:1-19:15</reference>) when prophesying of this very period of Jewish history. Zechariah connects his prophecy here with the older one of Jeremiah: showing the further application of the same divine threat against his unfaithful people in their destruction under Rome, as before in that under Nebuchadnezzar. Hence <reference osisRef="Matt.27.9">Mt 27:9</reference>, in English Version, and in the oldest authorities, quotes Zechariah's words as Jeremiah's, the latter being the original author from whom Zechariah derived the groundwork of the prophecy. Compare the parallel case of <reference osisRef="Mark.1.2">Mr 1:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.3">3</reference> in the oldest manuscripts (though not in English Version), quoting Malachi's words as those of "Isaiah," the original source of the prophecy. Compare my Introduction to Zechariah. The "potter" is significant of God's absolute power over the clay framed by His own hands (<reference osisRef="Isa.45.9">Is 45:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.18.6">Jr 18:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.9.20">Ro 9:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.9.21">21</reference>).<div eID="gen24827" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24828" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in the house of the Lord--</hi>The thirty pieces are thrown down in the temple, as the house of Jehovah, the fit place for the money of Jehovah-Messiah being deposited, in the treasury, and the very place accordingly where Judas "cast them down." The thirty pieces were cast "to the potter," because it was to him they were "appointed by the Lord" ultimately to go, as a worthless price (compare <reference osisRef="Matt.27.6">Mt 27:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.7.10">7, 10</reference>). For "I took," "I threw," here Matthew has "they took," "they gave them"; because their (the Jews' and Judas') act was all His "appointment" (which Matthew also expresses), and therefore is here attributed to Him (compare <reference osisRef="Acts.2.23">Ac 2:23</reference>; 4:28). It is curious that some old translators translate, for "to the potter," "to the treasury" (so Maurer), agreeing with <reference osisRef="Matt.27.6">Mt 27:6</reference>. But English Version agrees better with Hebrew and <reference osisRef="Matt.27.10">Mt 27:10</reference>. <div eID="gen24828" type="x-p"/>

The breaking of the bond of union between Judah and Israel's ten tribes under Rehoboam is here the image used to represent the fratricidal discord of factions which raged within Jerusalem on the eve of its fall, while the Romans were thundering at its gates without. entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13166"/><div sID="gen24830" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13166"/><hi type="bold">15. yet--</hi>"take again"; as in <reference osisRef="Zech.11.7">Zec 11:7</reference> previously he had taken other implements.<div eID="gen24830" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24831" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">instruments--</hi>the accoutrements, namely, the shepherd's crook and staff, wallet, &c. Assume the character of a bad ("foolish" in Scripture is synonymous with wicked, <reference osisRef="Ps.14.1">Psa 14:1</reference>) shepherd, as before thou assumedst that of a good shepherd. Since the Jews would not have Messiah, "the Good Shepherd" (<reference osisRef="John.10.11">Joh 10:11</reference>), they were given up to Rome, heathen and papal, both alike their persecutor, especially the latter, and shall be again to Antichrist, the "man of sin," the instrument of judgment by Christ's permission. entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13168"/><div sID="gen24839" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13168"/><hi type="bold">17. the idol--</hi>The Hebrew expresses both vanity and an idol. Compare <reference osisRef="Isa.14.13">Is 14:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.11.36">Da 11:36</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Thess.2.4">2Th 2:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.13.5">Re 13:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.13.6">6</reference>, as to the idolatrous and blasphemous claims of Antichrist. The "idol shepherd that leaveth the flock" cannot apply to Rome, but to some ruler among the Jews themselves, at first cajoling, then "leaving" them, nay, destroying them (<reference osisRef="Dan.9.27">Da 9:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.11.30-Dan.11.38">11:30-38</reference>). God's sword shall descend on his "arm," the instrument of his tyranny towards the sheep (<reference osisRef="2Thess.2.8">2Th 2:8</reference>); and on his "right eye," wherewith he ought to have watched the sheep (<reference osisRef="John.10.12">Joh 10:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.10.13">13</reference>). However, Antichrist shall destroy, rather than "leave the flock." Perhaps, therefore, the reference is to the shepherds who left the flock to Antichrist's rapacity, and who, in just retribution, shall feel his "sword" on their "arm," which ought to have protected the flock but did not, and on their "eye," which had failed duly to watch the sheep from hurt. The blinding of "the right eye" has attached to it the notion of ignominy (<reference osisRef="1Sam.11.2">1Sa 11:2</reference>). <chapter eID="Zech.11"/>
